title: How dialysis cleans blood: diffusion and fluid removal
intro: Dialysis removes some waste products and excess water when kidneys cannot do enough. It supports balance rather than washing all substances out of blood. It does not replace every kidney function, so medicines, nutrition and monitoring remain important.

sections.heading: A selective membrane
paragraphs: Blood and dialysis fluid are separated by a membrane that lets selected small substances cross while normally retaining blood cells and many large proteins. The fluid’s composition is chosen carefully; dialysis is not a simple exchange with plain water.

sections.heading: Diffusion
paragraphs: Particles move according to concentration differences. Keeping suitable dialysis fluid on the other side of the membrane helps remove waste and adjust salts. Treatment settings depend on the person’s blood chemistry; faster removal is not always safer.

sections.heading: Removing water
paragraphs: Ultrafiltration moves water across the membrane using pressure differences. Removing too much too quickly may cause low blood pressure or cramps. The team uses examination, weight and symptoms to set a suitable plan, not just thirst or ankle appearance.

sections.heading: Two main approaches
paragraphs: Hemodialysis uses an external filter and vascular access. Peritoneal dialysis uses the abdominal lining and fluid exchanged through a catheter. Schedules, infection precautions and daily demands differ; neither should be selected from a mechanism diagram alone.

sections.heading: Practical safety
paragraphs: Attend prescribed treatment and report illness or missed sessions promptly. Follow individual diet, fluid and access instructions. Severe breathlessness, chest pain, collapse or uncontrolled access bleeding requires emergency help; fever or cloudy peritoneal fluid needs urgent team advice. Before a consultation, note when a symptom began, what makes it better or worse, and how it affects ordinary activities. Bring previous reports if available. Ask the professional to connect the explanation to your own findings rather than assuming that a general description establishes a diagnosis.
